entry.title: Using a Raspberry Pi as a Home Router
entry.summary:
This article walks you through how to use your Raspberry Pi (RPi) as a home router. The central problem being solved is: How to use a RPi’s wireless interface as a Wi‑Fi access point that is connected to the Internet via the RPi’s Ethernet port. The solution relies heavily on NetworkManager’s shared connection mode. Your RPi: Is running Raspberry Pi OS based on Debian Bookworm (or later) Has a working Internet connection via its Ethernet port Manages network connections using NetworkManager eth0 is correctly configured
Run: sudo nmcli device
Confirm that device eth0 is in the connected state. # Create Wi‑Fi connection # Of course you need to replace `wlan0` # with your interface name sudo nmcli connection add type wifi \ ifname wlan0 \ con-name ap0 \ ssid "<ACCESS-POINT-NAME>" \ autoconnect yes
# Set access point mode sudo nmcli connection modify ap0 \ 802-11-wireless.mode ap
# Use 2.4 GHz band sudo nmcli connection modify ap0 \ 802-11-wireless.band bg
# Set WPA2/WPA3 pre‑shared key sudo nmcli connection modify ap0 \ wifi-sec.key-mgmt wpa-psk \ wifi-sec.psk "<PASSWORD-GOES-HERE>"
NetworkManager’s shared mode: Starts a DHCP server on the interface Enables IP forwarding Enables IP masquerading (NAT)
# Enable shared mode sudo nmcli connection modify ap0 \ ipv4.method shared
# Specify IPv4 subnet sudo nmcli connection modify ap0 \ ipv4.addresses 172.18.0.1/24
# Disable IPv6 (optional) sudo nmcli connection modify ap0 \ ipv6.method ignore
sudo nmcli connection up ap0
# Check Wi‑Fi access point gateway IP ip -4 addr show wlan0
# Check routes # Expect: # - 172.18.0.0/24 via wlan0 # - default route via eth0 ip -4 route
# Connected devices at the Wi‑Fi (L2) layer sudo iw dev wlan0 station dump
# Connected devices at the IP (L3) layer ip neigh show dev wlan0
Ubuntu Documentation – NetworkManager Shared Connections
Ubuntu Documentation – Configure Wi‑Fi Access Points

entry.title: Refactoring Your Classes with Clprolf and `indef_obj`
x402: Turning HTTP 402 into a Real Payment Primitive
entry.summary:
HTTP has carried the status code 402 – Payment Required since the early days of the web. The idea was simple: servers could charge per request. The reason it never worked wasn’t conceptual, it was infrastructural. Payments were slow, expensive, and required accounts, sessions, and chargeback-heavy intermediaries. x402 revisits this idea with modern primitives: stablecoins, fast settlement, and programmable authorization. The result is a web-native payment protocol that lets services charge for access directly in the HTTP request–response loop.
A client (human or agent) requests a resource. The server responds with HTTP 402 plus payment metadata:
token amount chain destination address The client signs a permit-style authorization using transferWithAuthorization (EIP-3009). A facilitator …
